--- pagetitle: Binomial Trend Detection - Identifying Ongoing Shifts in Data description-meta: Learn how the binomial trend detection method can identify ongoing trends in data over time by comparing week-over-week changes. This approach provides a statistical basis for detecting trends and overcoming the limitations of traditional rolling averages. toc: false lightbox: true execute: freeze: auto --- # Binomial Trend Detection Detecting trends and anomalies can be challenging, but rolling average benchmarking is a common method that smooths out fluctuations by comparing each new data point to the average of a specified number of previous values. While a rolling average can help highlight a metric trend, it can have limitations: - Sensitivity to window size - Lag in response - Difficulty accounting for varying granularities of seasonality or sudden changes An alternative method that can help identify ongoing shifts in trends over time is the **binomial trend detection approach**, which uses week-over-week (WoW) comparisons to detect changes. The binomial method analyzes week-over-week changes in data using a 14-day rolling window. It counts the number of days with positive or negative changes within this window and applies the binomial distribution to assess the probability of a consistent trend. A predefined threshold, such as 12 successes out of 14 trials (days) in the same direction, is used to identify statistically significant trends. | **Step** | **Details** | |----|----| | **Calculate WoW Deltas** | Compute week-over-week changes (deltas) for the metric of interest, determining whether the metric has increased or decreased each day. | | **Rolling 2-Week Window** | Analyze data within a 14-day rolling window, smoothing out short-term fluctuations while responding to recent changes. | | **Counting Positive and Negative Days** | Count the number of days with positive or negative WoW deltas within the 14-day window to assess recent performance trends. | | **Binomial Distribution** | Treat each day as an independent trial with a 50% chance of being positive or negative, using the binomial distribution for statistical analysis. | | **Trend Threshold** | Set a threshold for statistical significance (e.g., 12 or more positive/negative days out of 14) to ensure the trend is consistent and not random. | : Method Steps {.striped} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code .code-overflow-wrap} binom.test(12, 14, 1/2, alternative = "greater") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Exact binomial test data: 12 and 14 number of successes = 12, number of trials = 14, p-value = 0.00647 alternative hypothesis: true probability of success is greater than 0.5 95 percent confidence interval: 0.6146103 1.0000000 sample estimates: probability of success 0.8571429 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code .code-overflow-wrap code-fold="true"} library(ggplot2) library(showtext) library(ggtext) showtext_auto() showtext_opts(dpi = 300) font_add_google(name = "Roboto", family = "Roboto") font_1 <- "Roboto" n <- 14 p <- 1/2 x_obs <- 12 binom_test <- binom.test(x_obs, n, p, alternative = "greater") p_value <- binom_test$p.value conf_int <- binom_test$conf.int p_ge_x_obs <- sum(dbinom(x_obs:n, size = n, prob = p)) data <- data.frame( x = 0:n, probability = dbinom(0:n, size = n, prob = p), color = ifelse(0:n >= x_obs, "#C0392B", "#30394F") ) binom_visual <- ggplot(data, aes(x = x, y = probability, fill = color)) + geom_bar(stat = "identity") + scale_fill_identity() + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:n) + labs( title = "Binomial Distribution (n = 14, p = 0.5)", x = "Number of Successes", y = "Probability" ) + theme_minimal() + theme( panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.margin = margin(10, 10, 10, 10, "mm"), axis.text = element_text(family = font_1, size = 7), axis.title = element_text(family = font_1, size = 7), axis.title.x = element_text(margin = margin(5, 0, 0, 0, 'mm')), axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(0, 5, 0, 0, 'mm')), plot.title = element_text(family = font_1, size = 10) ) + annotate( geom = 'richtext', x = n+1, y = max(data$probability) * 0.9, label = paste0( "", "Threshold ≥ 12 trials (days)", "
", "P(X ≥ ", x_obs, ") = ", round(p_ge_x_obs, 4), "
", "95% CI = [", round(conf_int[1], 4), ", ", round(conf_int[2], 4), "]"), hjust = 1, fill = NA, label.color = NA ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell .fig-column-page lightbox='{"group":"plot"}'} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/binom-visual-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: This binomial approach improves upon rolling averages by offering better responsiveness to recent trends and reducing sensitivity to day-of-week variations, leading to more reliable trend detection.
